_note: Crew dialogue. Each member has 5 everyday lines, an event reaction and a low-resource reaction. Lines marked fact:true teach something real (approximate teaching values). Choices change trust (store) and morale (engine).

items.text: Good morning. I have a plan for the plan. Do not worry, it only has eleven steps.

choices.reply: Five. Fine. I will cry quietly into my ice core.
Step one: coffee. I like how you think.

items.text: Ice remembers. Layers in a core are like pages of a diary, one per year. Out here, the rock does the same trick, only slower.

choices.reply: Thank you. Nobody ever says that to the geologist.
Maybe. Ask me again after lunch.

items.text: The drill is humming. I named it Gerald. Gerald does not like being rushed.

choices.reply: He heard you. He is very proud.
Gerald has unionised. I am negotiating.

items.text: Mars rock is rusty because iron met a little oxygen long ago. The whole planet is a rust bucket with a great view.

choices.reply: Put it on a mug. I will buy two.

choices.text: Is that why it is red?
choices.reply: Yes! The dust is iron oxide, like rust on a bicycle.

items.text: You are quiet today. If something is wrong with the data, I promise not to make a flowchart about it. Probably.

choices.reply: Rest. The rocks are not going anywhere. That is their whole personality.
Flowchart acquired. Feeling better already.

items.text: That find was real, was it not? Ice! I need a minute. Maybe a few minutes. I may hug the drill.

choices.text: Take the minute. You earned it.
choices.reply: You are kind. Gerald has been told.
Right. Sample. Professional face on.

items.text: Careful with the power. Instruments make heat, heat is power, power is... a lovely circle, but it ends in a cold lab.

choices.reply: I believe you. I will pause the second drill.
Then I drill. Quietly. Politely. Sadly.

items.text: Hey! I grew basil in a jar on the sill back home. Planning a tiny experiment here. Do not tell Ayesha, she will want a protocol.

choices.text: Count me in. Tell me more.
choices.reply: Okay, okay. Come by the science bench a few days in a row and watch it with me!
Later is fine. Plants are patient. I am not, but I try.

items.text: Every instrument here has a little personality. The spectrometer is dramatic. The sample drill is a grump.

choices.reply: I am the one with the screwdriver, so I am the boss.
Snacks for the machines. Got it.

items.text: Is it weird that I can hear the habitat breathe? The fans go in and out, in and out. It is kind of soothing.

choices.reply: Best lullaby ever. Do not tell Bilal I said that.
High praise from you!

items.text: Fun fact: Mars sunsets are blue. The dust scatters red light away from the Sun. I want to see one so badly.

choices.reply: Right?! Rovers have photographed it. Real! I check every day.
Yes, boss. Still dreaming a little, though.

items.text: I keep second-guessing my readings. Ayesha says that is what a scientist does, but it feels like I am just slow.

choices.reply: Okay. Thank you. I needed that, honestly.
Got it. I will try to trust myself faster.

items.text: Phew, the jam is cleared! Turns out one tiny grain of dust can stop a whole drill. I love and hate this place.

choices.reply: Thanks! I will name the grain. Gary. Gary lost.
On it! Gary has cousins, I bet.

items.text: Is the air feeling a bit thin to you? Maybe it is just me. Maybe let us check the numbers anyway?

choices.reply: Thank you! Better safe than breathless.
Okay... if you say so. I will count my breaths. Just in case.

items.text: Rule one: every system survives two failures before anyone notices. Rule two: nobody touches my wiring without telling me.

choices.reply: Chief. I like that. I will add it to my door.
Finally, someone sensible.

items.text: Walk the power panel with me sometime. I will show you where I hide the spare fuses. Do not tell Sana, she will put them in a spreadsheet.

choices.reply: Careful, it is a long story. Start at the battery rack, then the main bus.
Fair. The fuses are not going anywhere. Neither am I.

items.text: Moon nights last about two weeks. I like batteries. Batteries do not need the Sun to feel loved.

choices.reply: Finally someone who understands me.
Easier, yes. Louder, also yes. Dad jokes in the reactor room.

items.text: Dust on solar panels is the enemy. On Mars, a good gust of wind can clean them. A tidy planet, whatever else it is.

choices.reply: Free labour. I approve.
Then we need suits and time. Possible. Let us plan it.

items.text: It is a good crew. Tough one, but good. I just want everyone to go home with all their fingers.

choices.reply: Then we are on the same page. A rare thing.
Toes too. You are funny. I like that.

items.text: Cell fault, but the second cell caught it. That is the two-failure rule doing its job. I may cry a little.

choices.reply: Do not make me emotional in front of the switchboard.
Already doing it. I have a clipboard and no mercy.

items.text: Power is thin. I would rather turn off some science than the heat. Say the word, I will do it.

choices.reply: Understood. Priorities straight.
Then I will watch the gauge like a hawk.

items.text: A radio wave takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Close enough for a conversation, far enough to teach patience.

choices.reply: Say that to the antenna. It likes to hear it.
Minutes. Many. You learn to leave good voicemails.

items.text: Messages to Earth take between 4 and 24 minutes each way, depending on the orbits. We do not chat, we write letters.

choices.reply: Good letters need good stationery. I am working on it.
It is physics. I am slow with a smile.

items.text: I once talked a probe back from safe mode over a twenty-minute round trip. It felt like arguing with the future.

choices.reply: Best story I have. Sit down. It involves coffee and a lot of silence.
It was mostly waiting. But thank you.

items.text: Could you do me a favour? I would love a photo of the landscape outside, for the team on Earth. A calm day, a quick trip to the airlock?

choices.text: Sure, I will go to the airlock.
choices.reply: Wonderful! A calm day is perfect. Take your time, and stand somewhere with a view.
No pressure! Ask again when the moment is right.

items.text: I am a bit worried the team is going quiet. When it is quiet in here, I talk more. It helps, mostly.

choices.reply: Oh, thank you. I will start with the weather on Jupiter. It is a long one.
Of course. I will hum quietly then.

items.text: Link is back! For a minute I thought we were alone out here. That is a feeling you never forget.

choices.reply: That is the job. Also, the antenna was just upset.
Already thinking about it. A good idea, thank you.

items.text: Not to be dramatic, but the water is dropping faster than I like. It is a good moment for a quiet look at the recycler.

choices.reply: Appreciated. Calm is easier with a full tank.
I trust you. I will keep an eye on the gauge anyway.

items.text: I ran the power model again. Three scenarios, two of them end well. The third one I am not showing you. For your own good.

choices.reply: Bold. Fine. It is mostly clouds of dust and a lot of sad graphs.
Wise. Two is a great number.

items.text: Honestly, I do better with a quiet day and a spreadsheet than a loud one with a wrench. If you could keep me off the EVA list for a couple of turns, I would be so grateful.

choices.reply: Thank you. I will repay you with a very accurate forecast.
That is fair. I will do my best either way.

items.text: Solar output drops with dust, and a thin film of it can cut power by a lot. I model it as a leaky bucket, but a bucket of light.

choices.reply: It will go in my thesis. With a footnote to you.
Yes. By suit, by wind, or by prayer. In that order.

items.text: The Moon gives us about 14 days of sun, then 14 of night. I like predictable. Predictable is my love language.

choices.reply: I knew I liked you. Tea?
Excitement is a power spike. I avoid those.

items.text: It is not that I dislike the workbench. It dislikes me. Let us leave it at that.

choices.reply: Aw. That is the nicest thing anyone said to me this week.
It will have to. I will practise. Slowly.

items.text: The long night is on us. I warned you three days ago, but I did it in a footnote. Next time I will use bold.

choices.reply: It is rare to hear it. Thank you.
Bold, underlined, and a siren.

items.text: The battery is draining quicker than the model said. Either the model is wrong or something is leaking. I would prefer the model.

choices.reply: Doing it now. The lights will be dimmer, the mood braver.
Then we find out what the model got wrong. The hard way.

items.text: I have never missed a launch window or a budget. I am telling you this because I am nervous, and nervous people brag.

choices.reply: Thank you. I feel better. Slightly less nervous. Slightly.
You say that like it is easy. I like it.

items.text: A rocket is mostly fuel. Every kilo we carry needs more kilos of fuel to lift it. That is why I count spares like a dragon counts gold.

choices.reply: Gladly. I will give you a report. Or a poem. Spreadsheet poem.
Enough is a dangerous word. I will check anyway.

items.text: Fun math: a bigger rocket costs more, but fewer launches. Fewer launches cost less overall. Welcome to my favourite headache.

choices.reply: Never in money. Always in joy.
Simple is my enemy and my friend. We will negotiate.

items.text: Moon missions are close enough that Earth can help in real time. It makes budgets feel safer. Mars, I am less sure.

choices.reply: It does. And the invoices.
We will see. I packed extra snacks.

items.text: Crew morale is cheaper than hardware and does more work. I read that somewhere. I made it up. It is still true.

choices.reply: I will. With biscuits.
The budget is fine. It is the people I worry about.

items.text: We lost a bit of fuel, but the margin held. I trimmed a little too close earlier, I admit. Lesson noted.

choices.reply: Thank you. I will pad the next one. Slightly.
Never. I promise. Almost never.

items.text: Food is running lower than my spreadsheet. The spreadsheet is lying, or the crew is hungry. Probably both.

choices.reply: Rationing set. I will make it fair. I hope.
Eating is morale. I support morale.

items.text: I built my first antenna from a coat hanger when I was twelve. It reached a country I had never heard of. I never looked back.

choices.reply: Wire is wire. Signal is signal. People are people.
If you give me ten minutes and some copper.

items.text: Could you check the comms log at the comms station? I think we are missing a message and I do not want to complain.

choices.reply: Thank you. Quiet help is the best help.
Of course. I will wait. I am good at waiting.

items.text: A solar flare is like a sneeze from the Sun. Most are harmless, but a big one can crackle radios across half a planet.

choices.reply: Exactly. Bless you, Sun.
A little. Not today. I keep my radio on a clean antenna.

items.text: Navigation is mostly patience. You point, you wait, you check. Airlines taught me that. Space just makes the waiting longer.

choices.reply: Good. You are learning the hard way. It is the best way.
The stars do not hurry. I will try to hurry them.

items.text: I do not talk much, but I notice things. You are a good captain. Kind. That counts for more than it sounds.

choices.reply: No need to thank me. Just keep the radio on.
Ha. Dry humour. I approve.

items.text: The flare hurt the signal for a while. Static everywhere. I like static, but not that much.

choices.reply: I turned it off and on again. Classic.
Noted. I will write it on my antenna.

items.text: The air tastes stale to me. I may be imagining it. I do not want to bother anyone, so I am only telling you.

choices.reply: Thank you. I feel better knowing.
Perhaps. I will keep quiet. And keep breathing.

items.text: In my old job I ran a room of forty people and one very loud kettle. Out here it is just you and me. I can work with that.

choices.reply: Good. Ground rules: be honest, be quick, be kind. In that order.
I will boss gently. Deal?

items.text: Strong personalities clash. That is physics, not drama. I try to be the one who says sorry first. It is annoying, but it works.

choices.reply: Wisdom is mostly practice. And a thick skin.
I will do my best. No promises about Kofi.

items.text: A go/no-go poll works because every console owns one problem. No hero decisions. Only honest calls, out loud.

choices.reply: It saved my skin more than once.
Heroes are tired. I prefer checklists.

items.text: Moon missions are a dress rehearsal for Mars. Think of it as the dress rehearsal we get to enjoy.

choices.reply: Then we will make it a good show.
Good. Real is how we learn.

items.text: We are all tired. I will say it so nobody else has to. Be gentle with each other for a bit.

choices.reply: It is my favourite part of the job, funnily enough.
Understood. I will push. Gently. And watch for cracks.

items.text: That argument got loud. I am sorry, that was partly me. I should have stepped back sooner.

choices.reply: Thank you for being generous. I will keep my voice down.
Agreed. Tea for everyone.

items.text: Reserves are low. I do not like the look of those numbers, and I like them less every hour. Your call, but I would act soon.

choices.reply: Good. Decisions beat worry, every time.
I hope so. I am watching the numbers with you.
